summary: AI-Powered Data Analytics has the right shape for Indian entry-level analyst hiring: SQL, spreadsheets, cleaning, pandas, dashboards, statistics, AI checking and storytelling, with sound questions and correct answer keys. It can't publish yet. No final question has a skill tag, and spreadsheets has only one final question to tag, so the Assessment Architect must tag all 15 and add a spreadsheets question. The final is also easier than the quizzes and gives almost no feedback, and seven questions test things no card teaches (correlation, $ references, NULLs, & filters, SUMIFS, LAG). The bigger teaching gap is the Course Architect's: every Learn card is under 80 words with few worked examples, no task gives the learner any data, and paid or Windows-only tools (Copilot, Python in Excel, Power BI Desktop) appear with no free route. The blueprint of 21 October already wrote most of the assessment fixes; they were never copied into the file.
strengths: All 55 answer keys are right, and the code answers behave as claimed (the blueprint ran them on pandas 3.0.6 and SQLite). Keep the code-option style: complete-looking options, each with one realistic mistake.
Indian, decision-led scenarios throughout (UPI, COD returns, Diwali data, kirana, clinics, coaching), and a clear thread of checking numbers before sharing them, AI-drafted ones included.
The DPDP wording in da-m09 card 3 matches Section 4 of the Act exactly (lawful purpose, with consent or for certain legitimate uses).
A field-specific project rubric (framing, data quality, analysis, dashboard, recommendation) and a realistic portfolio project brief.

findings.problem: Publish check: no final question has a "skill", so the Foundation assessment has 0 questions for data-literacy (trained by foundation module da-m01). Two questions already test it: da-f01 (framing) and da-f09 (mean versus median, taught in da-m01 card 3).
findings.fix: Add "skill": "data-literacy" to da-f01 and da-f09. Tag every other final question too (full map in the spreadsheets finding below).

findings.problem: Publish check: spreadsheets (foundation, da-m02) has no tagged final question. Only one final question tests spreadsheets at all (da-f03), so tagging alone cannot reach 2. The blueprint's coverage plan also leaves spreadsheets at one question (f03), so applying the blueprint as written would still fail publishing.
findings.fix: Tag the replacement da-f03 (the blueprint's "The SKUs that won't match") "skill": "spreadsheets". Replace da-f07 (INNER JOIN recall, already covered by da-m05-q1 and da-f12) with this spreadsheets question, keeping id da-f07. title "The pivot table that won't add up"; scenario "A Surat textile wholesaler pastes 6,000 order lines into Google Sheets and builds a pivot table of order_value by city. The pivot table shows a count of order_value, and switching it to SUM gives 0 for every city. The column holds entries like \"₹1,250\" and \"1,250 \"."; question "What should you do so the pivot table shows each city's total?"; options "Convert order_value to numbers (strip ₹, commas, spaces), then refresh" (right) / "Change the summary from SUM to AVERAGE, which works on text and numbers alike" / "Format the order_value column as Currency (₹), so the sheet reads it as money" / "Add order_value to Rows as well as Values, so each amount is visible"; explanation "SUM ignores text, and an entry with a ₹ sign or a trailing space is text, not a number. Once the column holds real numbers, the pivot table can add it."; why_wrong "AVERAGE also skips text, so it fails in the same way; a currency format changes how a number looks but does not turn text into a number; putting the amount in Rows lists each value instead of totalling it."; learning_outcome "A pivot table can only add a column stored as numbers."; difficulty Intermediate; topic "Text stored as numbers"; skill "spreadsheets". Full tag map: f01 data-literacy, f02 visualisation (blueprint replacement "The red stores"), f03 spreadsheets, f04 data-cleaning, f05 data-cleaning, f06 sql, f07 spreadsheets, f08 sql, f09 data-literacy, f10 statistics, f11 statistics (blueprint replacement, Expert), f12 python, f13 visualisation, f14 ai-analytics, f15 storytelling. Each foundation skill then has exactly 2, and every skill has at least 1.

findings.problem: Publish check: data-cleaning (foundation, da-m03) has no tagged final question.
findings.fix: Tag da-f04 and da-f05 "skill": "data-cleaning". If da-f04 is replaced by the blueprint's "The AI's cleaning step" (drop_duplicates on student_name), keep the tag data-cleaning: the judgement tested is which rows count as duplicates.

findings.problem: Publish check: sql (foundation, da-m04) has no tagged final question.
findings.fix: Tag da-f06 and da-f08 "skill": "sql". (da-f07 becomes the spreadsheets question above, so sql keeps 2.) da-f08 depends on LAG being taught in da-m05 (see the progression findings).

findings.problem: The final is easier than the module quizzes and doesn't combine modules. All 15 questions have no scenario. Difficulty is 5 Beginner, 7 Intermediate, 3 Advanced and 0 Expert (9.33 marks a question, against 9.63 in the quizzes). Four repeat a quiz point or are pure recall: da-f02 repeats da-m01-q2; da-f04 repeats da-m03-q1; da-f11 asks what df.shape returns; da-f15 repeats da-m10-q1. This is the Foundation certificate test, so it must place students fairly.
findings.fix: Apply the blueprint's MJ-1 replacements as written, keeping ids: f02 "The red stores", f03 "The SKUs that won't match", f04 "The AI's cleaning step", f11 "The checkout test, city by city" (Expert) and f15 "The memo's first line". Add the new f07 from the spreadsheets finding. Give f01, f05, f06, f08, f09, f10, f12, f13 and f14 a 2- to 3-sentence scenario set in an Indian business, so each is judged in context. Aim for about 4 Beginner, 6 Intermediate, 4 Advanced and 1 Expert, so the mean marks a question are above the quizzes'.

findings.problem: Adding to check.mjs's finding: 14 of the 15 final questions have no why_wrong, and none has a learning_outcome. The grader shows both to students. Ready-made text is in the blueprint (MJ-2 table), but it was never copied into the file.
findings.fix: Copy the blueprint's MJ-2 why_wrong and learning_outcome lines into f01, f05, f06, f08, f09, f10, f12, f13 and f14. Use the MJ-1 texts for the replaced questions and the text above for the new f07. Each why_wrong names each wrong option's mistake and doesn't start with "They" or "The others".

findings.problem: da-f05 option "Fill the blanks with 0, so that every respondent is included in the average satisfaction score" says satisfaction score, but the question is about average income. The copy error makes the option wrong for the wrong reason.
findings.fix: Change the option to "Fill the blanks with 0, so that every respondent is included in the average income".

findings.problem: da-f03 tests SUMIFS, and no module teaches SUMIF or SUMIFS. da-m02 teaches only tables, XLOOKUP and PivotTables, so the question is unfair.
findings.fix: Replace da-f03 with the blueprint's "The SKUs that won't match" (XLOOKUP failing on trailing spaces or text-stored SKUs), which combines da-m02 and da-m03 and needs no untaught function. Tag it spreadsheets.

findings.problem: da-f08 asks what LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) returns, but da-m05 card 3 only mentions "last month's value" and never names LAG (or LEAD). Interviewers in India ask about LAG often.
findings.fix: In da-m05 card 3, add a worked example: "LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) puts last month's revenue on this month's row, so revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) is the month-on-month change. LEAD looks one row ahead." Show a 3-row result (Jan ₹4.1 lakh / NULL, Feb ₹4.6 lakh / ₹4.1 lakh, Mar ₹4.3 lakh / ₹4.6 lakh). Also add the blueprint's note that a ROW_NUMBER() = 1 filter needs an outer query or CTE.

findings.problem: da-f08 asks for the definition of LAG, which is recall. Once da-m05 teaches LAG, the final should test using it.
findings.fix: Rewrite da-f08 as a scenario. A quick-commerce dark store's monthly_orders(month, orders) table; the manager wants the month-on-month change on each row. Options: "orders - LAG(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month)" (right) / "orders - LEAD(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month)" / "orders - LAG(orders) OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY month)" / "orders - SUM(orders) OVER (ORDER BY month)". why_wrong: LEAD subtracts next month; partitioning by month leaves one row per partition, so LAG is always NULL; SUM OVER subtracts the running total. Advanced.

findings.problem: da-m01-q4 (dark mode and test scores) tests correlation versus causation, and its explanation relies on a randomised test. Neither is taught in da-m01; randomisation comes only in da-m06. Aptitude item da-a15 also places correlation under data literacy.
findings.fix: Rename card 3 "Read numbers critically" and add a worked example after the ₹850 average: "Students who attend doubt-clearing sessions score 15% higher. Does attending cause it? Maybe keen students attend and also study more. Two things moving together can share a cause. Only a fair comparison, such as a test where some students are picked at random to attend, shows cause." Keep it under 160 words and split sentences over 20 words.

findings.problem: da-m01-q4: the explanation leans on "a randomised test", which da-m01 doesn't teach. The option "Ask for light-mode users' scores too…" is weak, because the comparison already includes them.
findings.fix: Explanation: "Keen, heavy users may be the ones who pick dark mode, and they would score higher anyway. Only a fair test, where some new users get dark mode by chance, shows whether the setting itself changes scores." Replace the light-mode option with "Agree, but switch it on first for the lowest scorers, since they have the most to gain" (why_wrong: "targeting low scorers still assumes the setting causes the scores").

findings.problem: da-m01 cards are 56, 51 and 46 words, below the house style's 80 to 160. None works through an example from start to finish: card 1 shows the reworded question but not how to get there, and card 2 names types but shows no table.
findings.fix: Card 1: work through "How are sales doing?" for a Pune bakery: who decides, which decision, what measure, which period, and the final question. Card 2: show a 6-column orders header (order_id, PIN code, order_date, city, payment_method, order_value), label each type, and show the common mistake: averaging PIN codes gives a number like 411,037 that means nothing. Card 3: see the progression finding. Each card 90 to 140 words.

findings.problem: da-m01 t2 ("List five columns you would expect…") is list work with no data, so the learner can't check their answer against anything.
findings.fix: Give the data in the task: "Here are the first 4 rows of a kirana store's UPI orders export: order_id, phone, PIN, order_date (stored as text, e.g. 05/04/2026), city, amount (e.g. \"₹1,250\"), payment_app." Ask: label each column's type, find the two stored as the wrong type, and say what would go wrong in a total or a sort. Hint unchanged.

findings.problem: da-m02-q4 tests absolute references ($F$1), which no card teaches.
findings.fix: Add to card 1 (or card 2) a worked example: "GST rate 18% is in F1. In C2 write =B2*$F$1 and fill it down. B2 becomes B3, B4…, but $F$1 stays fixed. Without the $ signs, row 3 would use F2, which is empty, and every result after row 2 would be 0." Name this as the common mistake.

findings.problem: da-m02-q4 is recall once taught ("What do the dollar signs do?"), and its card example would then match the question exactly.
findings.fix: Once the card uses GST, change the question's case to a commission rate in H1 for a Kochi electronics shop, and ask what goes wrong when =B2*H1 is filled down (answer: every row after the first uses an empty cell, so commissions show 0). Keep the distractors similar in length.

findings.problem: da-m02-q2 why_wrong says "the third option has the first two arguments swapped", but the swapped XLOOKUP is the second option. Option order can be reshuffled at any time, so position words go stale anyway.
findings.fix: Replace with: "VLOOKUP with TRUE does an approximate match, so it can quietly return the wrong category instead of \"New SKU\"; XLOOKUP(Master[SKU], B2, …) has the value and the lookup range swapped; SUMIF adds numbers and can't return a text category." Never name an option by position.

findings.problem: da-m02 cards are 46, 49 and 39 words. None works an example through to a result: card 3 says how to drag fields but never shows a finished pivot answering a question. SUMIFS, which Indian MIS roles use every day, isn't taught.
findings.fix: Card 2: a worked XLOOKUP on a 3-row price list, showing the result for a SKU that is missing ("Not found"), with VLOOKUP's approximate-match trap as the common mistake. Card 3: a worked pivot (Rows: payment method; Values: Average of Returned (1/0)) with its result, e.g. UPI 6%, COD 18%, and the mistake of using "% of column total". Add one line on SUMIFS as the formula route to the same totals. Each card 90 to 140 words.

findings.problem: da-m02 is the spreadsheet module, but neither task opens a spreadsheet. t1 asks the learner to "describe the PivotTable you would build", and t2 to write a formula with no data to test it on.
findings.fix: Link a free practice sheet (Google Sheets, 200 orders: order_date, city, category, payment_method, order_value, returned 1/0, sku) and a price-list tab. t1: build the pivot table and report the return rate for UPI and for cash on delivery. t2: write the XLOOKUP, fill it down, and report how many rows show "Not found". Both work in the free Google Sheets app or browser.

findings.problem: da-m02 says 90 minutes. check.mjs estimates 53 for the content as written (reading, two describe-only tasks, reflection and quiz).
findings.fix: After the cards and hands-on tasks above (about 4 minutes of reading and 25 to 30 minutes a task), 90 minutes is honest. If the tasks stay describe-only, cut to 60.

findings.problem: Adding to check.mjs's long-sentence finding: da-m02 teaches only Excel (Ctrl+T, Excel table syntax). Many students have only Google Sheets on a phone or old Excel in a college lab. XLOOKUP is not in Excel 2016 or 2019.
findings.fix: In card 1 add: "In Google Sheets: Format > Convert to table." In card 2 add: "XLOOKUP works in Google Sheets and Excel 2021 or later; it isn't in Excel 2016 or 2019." Split the 23- to 26-word sentences.

findings.problem: da-m02-q3 (return rate by payment method from a Returned column) reuses t1's scenario: an orders table, payment method, returned yes/no, return rate.
findings.fix: Give q3 a new context with the same skill: a coaching centre's enquiries sheet with a Converted column (1/0) and Source (Instagram, walk-in, referral) in Rows. Ask which Values setting shows each source's conversion rate. Keep the options parallel.

findings.problem: da-m03-q4 has a second defensible answer. The option "Nothing changes, because rows with no delivery time are simply left out of every average" is literally true: an average skips blanks whether or not you drop the rows.
findings.fix: Use the blueprint's MJ-4 rewrite of the question ("…how does the average delivery time you report compare with what customers actually experienced?"), its options and its why_wrong, in the new context from the rule-11 finding. Relabel it Intermediate (MJ-5): at present a learner with 3 of 4 right scores 20/35 and fails the module.

findings.problem: da-m03-q4 (food delivery, 8% missing delivery times) reuses t2's scenario (delivery dataset, 6% missing delivery times) with only the number changed.
findings.fix: Move q4 to a new context: a Hyderabad clinic's waiting-time log where 9% of rows have no "seen at" time, mostly patients who walked out after a long wait. Ask how the average waiting time compares with what patients experienced.

findings.problem: da-m03-q3 why_wrong says "a PivotTable treats each spelling as a different city". Stated that broadly, it isn't reliable: whether a pivot groups entries that differ only in capital letters depends on the tool.
findings.fix: Write: "a PivotTable doesn't merge different spellings such as Bengaluru, Bangalore and BLR".

findings.problem: da-m03 has no worked example (check.mjs), and its cards are 40, 57 and 45 words. Card 2 lists fixes in one sentence but never shows a cleaning log. Card 3 says missing data can bias a result but shows no numbers.
findings.fix: Card 2: work a 6-row example from a Jaipur coaching centre's enquiry list, showing before and after, and two log lines such as "Step 2: trimmed spaces in city, 41 rows changed" and "Step 3: mapped Bangalore/BLR/bangalore to Bengaluru, 212 rows". Name the free tools: TRIM and Data > Data cleanup in Google Sheets, Power Query in Excel. Card 3: show the numbers, e.g. 100 deliveries, 6 blank and all slow: the average of the rest is 28 minutes, but with them it would be 31. Each card 90 to 140 words.

findings.problem: da-m03 tasks are plans only. t1 writes a cleaning plan for a file the learner never sees, and t2 describes options. Neither produces a cleaned file or a log.
findings.fix: Give t1 a 30-row messy CSV (the hospital export described, with mixed date formats, department variants and "₹500" fees). Ask the learner to clean it in Google Sheets and submit the cleaned sheet plus a 5-line cleaning log with row counts. Keep t2 as reasoning, but give the numbers so the learner calculates both averages.

findings.problem: da-m03 says 90 minutes; check.mjs estimates 53 for the content as written.
findings.fix: With the hands-on t1 and the longer cards, 90 is honest. Otherwise cut to 60.

findings.problem: da-m04-q3 (= NULL against IS NULL) and da-m04-q4 (AVG skips NULLs) test NULL handling, which no da-m04 card teaches. da-m03 teaches "missing is not zero" only as an idea.
findings.fix: Add to card 3, or replace card 1's plain syntax line with: "A blank in a database is NULL, meaning unknown. Test it with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL; = NULL is never true. AVG, SUM and COUNT(column) skip NULLs; COUNT(*) counts every row." Add a worked 4-row example showing AVG(stars) = 4.0 over the 2 rated rows, not the 4.

findings.problem: da-m04-q4 explanation says "Summary functions skip NULLs", which is false for COUNT(*). Its right option is also the only one with a reason attached ("…; AVG ignores NULLs"), a clue the house style forbids.
findings.fix: Explanation: use the blueprint's MN-3 text ("AVG, like SUM and COUNT(stars), skips NULLs; only COUNT(*) counts every row…"). Right option: "The average of the 600 orders that have a rating". Give two wrong options a reason too, e.g. "The average across all 1,000 orders, with missing ratings counted as 0" and "Nothing useful, because NULLs make AVG return an error". Relabel Intermediate (MJ-5).

findings.problem: da-m04-q2 explanation is one short sentence (check.mjs). It is also a recall item with no scenario.
findings.fix: Give it a case: a Lucknow sweet-shop chain's orders table, where the owner wants cities with revenue above ₹10 lakh. Explanation: "WHERE filters rows before they are grouped, so the totals don't exist yet. HAVING filters after GROUP BY, so it can test SUM(order_value)."

findings.problem: da-m04 cards are 34, 42 and 41 words. They show queries but never the table a query returns, so a beginner can't picture the result. t1 filters April 2026, but no card warns about the date-range trap.
findings.fix: Card 1: show a 5-row orders table, the query, and its 2-row result. Card 2: show GROUP BY's output for the same rows. Add the common mistake: on a timestamp column, BETWEEN '2026-04-01' AND '2026-04-30' drops payments after midnight on 30 April; write paid_at >= '2026-04-01' AND paid_at < '2026-05-01'. Each card 90 to 140 words.

findings.problem: da-m04 tasks have no database to run on. The learner writes a query they can't test, so they never see an error message or a result.
findings.fix: Attach the payments table as a CSV and tell learners to run it free in the DuckDB shell (shell.duckdb.org runs in any browser, phone included, and the data stays on the device) or the BigQuery sandbox. t1: paste the query and its result. Hint: the half-open date range.

findings.problem: da-m04 says 90 minutes; check.mjs estimates 53 for the content as written.
findings.fix: With run-it-yourself tasks (setting up the CSV in the browser shell takes about 10 minutes the first time), 90 is honest. Otherwise cut to 60.

findings.problem: da-m05 has no worked example (check.mjs), and its cards are 50, 38 and 54 words. Card 2 states fan-out but shows no numbers. Card 1 says a LEFT JOIN "leaves blanks", but SQL shows NULL. The common trap of filtering an o. column in WHERE after a LEFT JOIN isn't named.
findings.fix: Card 1: say "NULL", and show a 3-customer example where one has no orders. Add the trap: WHERE o.order_date >= … after a LEFT JOIN drops the customers with no orders; put that condition in ON instead. Card 2: work it through: 3 orders worth ₹1,500, a customer with 2 addresses gives 6 rows and ₹3,000. Card 3: add LAG (see the da-f08 finding). Each card 90 to 140 words.

findings.problem: da-m05 t1 and t2 have no tables to run on, and t2 allows "describe (or write)".
findings.fix: Use the same free DuckDB or BigQuery route as da-m04, with customers.csv and orders.csv (include customers with no orders and some with 3 or more). t1: run the query and report how many 2026 sign-ups never ordered. t2: write it, and report the repeat share of April revenue. The blueprint's expected answer (number before filtering April) gives a checkable result.

findings.problem: da-m05 says 90 minutes; check.mjs estimates 53.
findings.fix: With run-on-data tasks, 90 is honest; otherwise 60.

findings.problem: da-m05-q1 (customers with no orders, LEFT JOIN + IS NULL) reuses t1's scenario and tables. da-m05-q3 repeats card 3's ROW_NUMBER line with names changed, so it tests recall.
findings.fix: q1: move to a new context, e.g. a college placement cell with students(student_id, branch) and applications(student_id, company): which students haven't applied anywhere? q3: use the blueprint's MN-6 rewrite ("Latest visit only", ORDER BY visit_date DESC), Intermediate.

findings.problem: da-m06 cards are 47, 57 and 52 words. Card 1 uses "standard deviation" without explaining it. No card works a number through, e.g. a new value against a usual range.
findings.fix: Card 1: either drop "standard deviation" or explain it in one line ("a typical distance from the average"). Work an example from a context the tasks don't use: a Bhopal clinic sees 110 to 150 patients a day for 8 weeks; 158 on Monday is just above the range, so watch for a week before calling it a change. Card 3: say what "a clear difference" means: decide the sample size and run length first, and check the gap against chance. Each card 90 to 140 words.

findings.problem: Adding to check.mjs: card 2 has a 36-word sentence ("…72% are satisfied…from 2,000 answers it is within a couple of points"). "Margin", "noise" and "standard deviation" are used without a plain explanation.
findings.fix: Split card 2's long sentence into three: "From 50 answers, 72% satisfied could really be anywhere from about 60% to 85%." "From 2,000 answers, it is within about 2 points." "Bigger samples give narrower ranges." Define "noise" the first time ("ordinary ups and downs").

findings.problem: da-m07-q4 tests combining pandas conditions with & and brackets, which no card teaches. Card 2 shows only a one-condition filter.
findings.fix: Add to card 2 or 3: df[(df["status"] == "success") & (df["amount"] > 5000)], with the rule "use & for and, | for or, and put brackets round each condition; Python's and raises an error on whole columns".

findings.problem: da-m07-q4: the option df.filter("success", 5000) doesn't look like real code (rule 2), and the item is labelled Advanced, though once taught it is everyday pandas.
findings.fix: Replace that option with df[(df["status"] == "success") & df["amount"] > 5000] (brackets missing round the second condition: & binds before >, so it errors or filters wrongly). why_wrong: "without brackets, & is applied before >". Relabel Intermediate (MJ-5).

findings.problem: da-m07 card 2 is a list of six commands with no worked case or output (31 words). Card 1 is a pitch. No card shows a short notebook working from question to answer, or the common mistakes. Rule 8: card 2 presents dayfirst=True as the fix, but the pandas docs warn it "is not strict"; format="%d/%m/%Y" is the strict choice. pandas 3.0 (January 2026) no longer supports the chained assignment that older tutorials use.
findings.fix: Card 2: work a 5-row UPI example from read_csv to a groupby result, showing the printed output. Use pd.to_datetime(df["txn_time"], format="%d/%m/%Y %H:%M"), and say dayfirst=True only "prefers" day-first. Card 3: add the pandas 3 note: "Change values with df.loc[rows, \"col\"] = …; the older df[df.x > 5][\"y\"] = 0 does nothing in pandas 3." Each card 90 to 140 words.

findings.problem: da-m07 t1 gives no file and allows "plain words", so a Python module can be completed without running any Python.
findings.fix: Link a 5,000-row fictional UPI CSV and a starter Google Colab notebook (free). t1: run the steps and report the top 5 categories by successful value, plus one check (row count before and after filtering). t2 is fine; add "run it on leads.csv and say how many rows drop_duplicates removed".

findings.problem: da-m07 says 120 minutes; check.mjs estimates 53, more than double.
findings.fix: With the hands-on notebook tasks, set 90. A first Colab session (sign-in, upload, run) needs about 10 extra minutes.

findings.problem: Card 1 offers "Python in Excel" beside Google Colab as if both were free. Microsoft says free and perpetual consumer licences don't support it, and it doesn't run on phones. Colab works in a phone browser but is awkward on a small screen.
findings.fix: Card 1: "Run it free in Google Colab in your browser. A laptop or a college computer makes it easier than a phone. (Python in Excel also exists, but it needs a paid Microsoft 365 plan.)"

findings.problem: da-m08 has no worked example (check.mjs). Card 3 does four jobs (Power BI connections, DAX measures, visual calculations, Copilot) in 59 words. The truncated axis, which q2 tests and t2 asks about, is never taught.
findings.fix: Card 1: add the common mistake with numbers: a bar axis starting at ₹99 lakh makes ₹102 lakh look three times ₹100 lakh. Card 2: describe one worked page for a fictional coaching chain (top: admissions against target per centre; middle: by-centre breakdown with red for below target; bottom: 12-week trend). Card 3: "Build it free": Looker Studio or Google Sheets charts (browser), or Power BI Desktop (free, Windows only), with one DAX measure as the example. Mention Copilot in one sentence as a paid feature some employers provide. Each card 90 to 140 words.

findings.problem: da-m08 t1 asks the learner to "describe one page", and t2 to describe a chart remembered from somewhere. Nothing is built, though building a dashboard is the module outcome and the overview outcome.
findings.fix: t1: build a one-page dashboard from the shared practice sheet in Looker Studio (free, browser) or Power BI Desktop (Windows), with 3 to 4 key numbers against targets, one breakdown and one trend; submit a link or screenshot. t2: give a bad chart (a 3D pie of 9 brands, with its data) to redraw in Google Sheets.

findings.problem: da-m08's summary ("check what Copilot drafts") and card 3 treat Copilot in Power BI as a normal step. Microsoft Learn says it needs a paid Fabric capacity (F2 or higher) or Premium P1; trial capacities, free SKUs and a Pro licence alone aren't enough. No free dashboard tool is taught, though the project allows Looker Studio.
findings.fix: Summary: "Choose the right chart, design dashboards around decisions, and check any number a tool drafts." Card 3 as in the explanation finding. Change the visualisation skill description to "…in Looker Studio, Google Sheets or Power BI".

findings.problem: da-m08 says 90 minutes; check.mjs estimates 53.
findings.fix: With a built dashboard (t1, about 35 to 40 minutes) and a redraw (t2), 90 is honest; otherwise 60.

findings.problem: Power BI Desktop is Windows only and needs at least a 1440x900 screen (Microsoft Learn), so phone and Mac learners can't follow card 3.
findings.fix: Lead with the browser route (Looker Studio or Sheets charts, which work on any device), and name Power BI Desktop as "free on a Windows computer, and what most Indian employers use".

findings.problem: da-m08-q2: an axis starting at ₹99 lakh makes the ₹102 lakh bar 3 times taller than ₹100 lakh, not "five times" (5 times needs ₹99.5 lakh). The scenario and the right option don't quite agree.
findings.fix: Scenario: "…but the new bar looks three times taller." Keep the right option "starts near ₹99 lakh".

findings.problem: da-m08-q1: "A pie chart" and "A donut chart" are the same mistake, so the question has only two real distractors. It is also a recall item with no scenario.
findings.fix: Add a case (a Nagpur pharmacy chain's owner wants to see whether revenue has been rising over 18 months), and replace the donut option with "A bar chart sorted by revenue" (why_wrong: "sorting by size breaks the time order").

findings.problem: da-m09 has no worked example (check.mjs). Card 2 lists the ways AI goes wrong but never shows one being caught.
findings.fix: Card 2: work one case from a context the tasks don't use. A prompt asks for "monthly active customers" for a Kochi pharmacy; the AI's SQL counts orders, not distinct customers. A hand count of 10 rows shows 7 customers where the query says 10, and adding COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) fixes it. Each card 90 to 140 words.

findings.problem: da-m09 t2 only describes how to check an AI summary; nothing is checked. t1 lists checks but never runs them.
findings.fix: t2: give a 20-row sales sheet and an AI summary with one planted error (Q2 dated April to July). The learner finds the error with a pivot table or SUMIFS and rewrites the sentence. t1: say "use any free AI assistant, with column names and made-up rows only", then run the 3 checks on the practice data.

findings.problem: Adding to check.mjs's long sentences (up to 36 words in cards 2 and 3): card 1 lists Copilot in Excel and Power BI beside free assistants without saying they are paid.
findings.fix: Card 1: "Free assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini can all do this. Copilot in Excel and Power BI does too, on paid plans some employers provide." Split every sentence over 20 words in cards 2 and 3.

findings.problem: da-m09 card 3 states the DPDP Act correctly (lawful purpose, with consent or for certain legitimate uses). It doesn't say the DPDP Rules, 2025 phase in, which learners will hear about at work.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: "The DPDP Rules, 2025 bring in the Act's duties in stages; most apply to organisations from May 2027, but careful handling starts now." Don't give a day: sources differ on 13 or 14 May 2027.

findings.problem: da-m09-q3: "Email the file to a friend who is good with AI…" is a joke option nobody who read the card would pick.
findings.fix: Replace it with "Replace names with initials, keep the phones and diagnoses, and paste it into a free chatbot" (why_wrong: "initials don't hide anyone while phone numbers and diagnoses stay").

findings.problem: da-m09-q1 why_wrong ("They leave out the table…, or both") doesn't say which option makes which mistake (rule 6).
findings.fix: Name each: "The first gives no columns and doesn't define a repeat customer; the expert-persona prompt gives neither the table nor the measure; \"my company database\" gives the assistant no schema to work from." Use descriptions, not positions.

findings.problem: da-m09-q1 (prompt for monthly repeat-customer SQL from orders) reuses t1's scenario (repeat customers each month from orders).
findings.fix: Give q1 a new measure and context, e.g. a bus-booking app's bookings(booking_id, user_id, route, booked_at, fare): which prompt is most likely to get correct SQL for average fare per route last month?

findings.problem: da-m09-q4 is labelled Advanced, but the judgement is straightforward once card 2 is read (blueprint MJ-5).
findings.fix: Relabel Intermediate.

findings.problem: da-m10 cards are 48, 43 and 39 words. Card 1 gives a good opening line but doesn't show a weak one turned into it. Card 3 says what to state but shows no example caveat.
findings.fix: Card 1: a before and after: "This report analyses six months of data from…" becomes "Recommendation: …", with a note on what moved and why. Card 3: show a one-line caveat: "Based on 14,000 customers, January to June 2026; customers chose the trial kit themselves, so a test would confirm it." Each card 90 to 140 words; split the 35-word sentence.

findings.problem: da-m10-q1 why_wrong ("They describe the work done…") and da-m10-q2 why_wrong ("They are facts…") group the wrong options instead of naming each one's mistake (rule 6). Both are also recall items with no scenario.
findings.fix: q1: give a case (a Tier-2 city footwear D2C brand's ops head, who has two minutes) and write one reason per option, e.g. "the row count says how big the work was, not what to do; …". q2: same, e.g. "₹640 compared with last year is a finding with no action; …".

findings.problem: Adding to check.mjs: card 1's example sentence is 35 words. CFO, COD and Tier-3 are used without explanation in the quiz.
findings.fix: Split card 1's example into two sentences. Write "finance head (CFO)" and "cash on delivery (COD)" the first time.

findings.problem: 17 module quiz questions have no scenario (house style: scenario-based): da-m01-q2, m02-q1, m03-q2, m03-q3, m04-q1, m04-q2, m05-q1, m05-q3, m05-q4, m06-q1, m07-q1, m07-q3, m07-q4, m08-q1, m09-q1, m10-q1, m10-q2. Several test recall of a card line.
findings.fix: Give each a 1- to 2-sentence case in a new Indian context (findings above cover m04-q2, m05-q1, m05-q3, m08-q1, m09-q1, m10-q1 and m10-q2). For short code items (m04-q1, m07-q1, m07-q3), one sentence naming the business and the table is enough.

findings.problem: da-m01-q3 explanation says the median is "roughly ₹2,200–2,500". With 47 of 50 fees between ₹2,000 and ₹2,500, the median can be anywhere in that range.
findings.fix: "…The median stays at what the middle student pays, between ₹2,000 and ₹2,500."

findings.problem: Several statements rate liking, feeling or knowledge, not behaviour: da-a05 ("I can summarise…quickly"), da-a10 ("I enjoy breaking a question…"), da-a11 ("I'm comfortable learning…syntax"), da-a14 ("I know an average can hide…"), da-a16 ("I like automating tasks"). da-a10 to da-a12 aren't about SQL at all.
findings.fix: Use the blueprint's MN-7 rewrites: a05 "I sort or filter a spreadsheet to find the rows I need, instead of scrolling through it."; a10 "When I need one number from a long list, I write down the steps (which rows, which groups, which total) before I start."; a11 "I look up the exact syntax of a formula or command instead of guessing it."; a12 (reversed) "When I need figures from a large table, I ask someone else to pull them for me."; a14 "When I see an average, I look at the highest and lowest values behind it."; a16 "When I repeat the same steps on a file every week, I look for a way to automate them."

findings.problem: Overview outcome 4 ("Use AI assistants to work faster, and verify everything they produce") isn't shown by any project deliverable. The da-m09 tasks use given scenarios, not the learner's own analysis. The brief also says nothing about protecting personal data in the business data a learner receives.
findings.fix: Add a deliverable: "An AI log: each prompt you used, what the AI produced, how you checked it, and what you changed (or \"no AI used\")." Add to the brief: "If a business shares data, get its written permission, remove names, phone numbers and other personal details before you analyse it, and never paste personal data into an AI tool."

findings.problem: The rubric descriptions are one-liners. None of them grades AI use and checking (outcome 4), or whether the learner can explain their own work, which is the defence against outsourced or AI-written projects. The blueprint has ready Competent-level lines and full 0 to 5 descriptors, but they were never copied in.
findings.fix: Replace the five descriptions with the blueprint's "Proposed one-line descriptions" (e.g. analysis: "Correct SQL or Python, joins checked, a key number reproduced; AI help disclosed and checked"; recommendation: "…and the learner can explain every step"). Give mentors the 0 to 5 table from the blueprint's Practical evidence section.

findings.problem: No overview outcome covers statistics, though da-m06, five quiz questions, the final and the analysis criterion all test it (blueprint gap G1).
findings.fix: Add an outcome: "Tell a real change from noise using samples, spread and simple A/B tests".

findings.problem: overview.hours is 35, but the file never states the project time. Modules add up to 14 hours and the final to 0.5, so the project is an implied 20.5 hours that no one can check. Module minutes will also change with the time findings above.
findings.fix: Say in the project brief "about 20 hours over 3 to 4 weeks with your mentor". After the module minutes are settled, set hours to (sum of module minutes / 60) + 20 + 0.5, rounded to a whole hour.

findings.problem: Skill descriptions name only paid or Windows routes: visualisation is "in Power BI or Excel", and ai-analytics is "Using AI assistants and Copilot".
findings.fix: visualisation: "Choosing the right chart and building dashboards around decisions, in Looker Studio, Google Sheets or Power BI." ai-analytics: "Using free AI assistants (and Copilot where an employer provides it) to speed up analysis, checking their output, and protecting personal data."

findings.problem: No task in the programme gives the learner data. All 20 tasks are plans, descriptions or lists, so the skills employers test (SQL, Excel, pandas, a dashboard) are never practised on a real file before the project.
findings.fix: Create one fictional practice dataset used across the modules: "Masala Mart", a D2C spice brand. orders.csv (2,000 rows, with dd/mm/yyyy dates, messy city spellings, "₹" amounts, a returned 1/0 column and some duplicate rows), customers.csv (with some customers who never ordered) and products.csv. Publish it as a view-only Google Sheet and as CSV files. Link it in the da-m02, m03, m04, m05, m07, m08 and m09 tasks, so each module adds a step on the same data.

findings.problem: The assessment blueprint doesn't match the file. Its question map and coverage map describe the final "after the corrections", which was never applied. Its coverage plan leaves spreadsheets with one final question (f03), so it would fail rule 13. The older -review.md says every question has a scenario, why_wrong and learning_outcome, which isn't true of the file.
findings.fix: After this round's fixes, update the blueprint's final table and coverage map to the file as it then stands: add a "skill" column using the tag map in the spreadsheets finding, and add the new f07. Mark ai-powered-data-analytics-review.md as superseded at its top.

findings.problem: Research: Indian junior analyst and MIS roles use SUMIFS/COUNTIFS daily, and some ask for Tableau. The programme teaches neither.
findings.fix: For Paul: consider one line on SUMIFS in da-m02 card 3 (see that finding), and naming Tableau Public as a free alternative in da-m08. No new module is needed.

lessons.rule: Before writing a quiz or final question, name the Learn-card sentence (in that module or an earlier one) it depends on. If there isn't one, add the teaching to the card or change the question.
lessons.why: In the Data Analytics programme, seven questions (da-m01-q4, m02-q4, m04-q3, m04-q4, m07-q4, f03, f08) tested correlation, $ references, NULLs, & filters, SUMIFS and LAG, which no card taught.

lessons.rule: Never refer to an option by its position ("the third option", "option B") in an explanation or why_wrong. Describe or quote it instead, because options are reshuffled to balance answer positions.
lessons.why: da-m02-q2's why_wrong said "the third option" for an option that was second after the positions were balanced.

lessons.rule: In a tools programme, give every Practise task a small dataset the learner can open free on a phone (a view-only Google Sheet or a CSV linked in the task), and ask for a result they can check. Allow at most one "describe what you would do" task per module.
lessons.why: All 20 Data Analytics tasks were plans or descriptions, so learners met their first real file only in the project.
